🪑 Sitting Allowed, Sitting Forbidden — why the Temple Mount watch stands inside the wall, and the courtyard watch stands outside
🧵 Sleeping on the Sacred Vestments — the kilayim problem, and several rounds of resolution

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Counting Watches, Guarding Modesty
overview.subtitle: Tamid 27a–27b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara first explains why young priests are called 'rovim' in one mishna and 'pirḥei khehunna' in another — a distinction of eligibility for service, not age alone. It then tackles the Levites' twenty-one Temple watch posts, reconciling them against a biblical verse that appears to list twenty-four, and explains why the Temple Mount's watch could sit (inside the wall) while the Temple courtyard's watch could not (outside the wall, since sitting there is reserved for Davidic kings). A lengthy analysis follows on whether priests could sleep with their vestments beneath their heads, given the diverse-kinds (kilayim) prohibition, before the Gemara turns to whether priestly garments may be enjoyed as ordinary clothing — illustrated by Shimon HaTzaddik's dramatic meeting with Alexander the Great. The daf closes with a story about bathroom etiquette and practical fatherly advice passed from Rav and Rav Huna to their sons.

slides.title: 🔢 Reconciling the Levites' Twenty-One Watch Posts
slides.subtitle: A biblical verse (I Chronicles 26:17–18) seems to count twenty-four
rows: Adds up to 24 watches, not the mishna's 21
'For the Asuppim two' is read as always exactly two — removing a repeated count, bringing the total closer
The Parbar watch (western side) had only ONE actual watchman; the second person mentioned merely kept him company since that post was isolated
Simply accept 24 as accurate: 3 of the watches are the PRIESTS' three posts, and 21 are the Levites'
But doesn't the verse say all 24 are Levites?

Per Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: in 24 places Scripture calls priests 'Levites' too (e.g., Ezekiel 44:15's 'the priests the Levites') — so 3 of the 24 are really priestly posts described with Levite terminology

slides.title: 🪑 Why Location Determines Who May Sit
slides.subtitle: Temple Mount watch (inside the wall) vs. Temple courtyard watch (outside)

nodes.content: ❓ Why do Levites keep watch INSIDE the Temple Mount's wall, but OUTSIDE the Temple courtyard's wall?
🪑 On the Temple Mount, sitting is permitted for anyone — so posting watchmen inside lets them sit and rest when tired
🚫 In the Temple courtyard, sitting is forbidden to everyone except kings of the House of David — so watchmen are stationed OUTSIDE the wall instead, where they're free to sit

🚪 Related dispute: how many gates did the courtyard actually have — 5, 7, or 8? Abaye: two gates (Spark, Hearth) needed no Levite watch since priests already guarded them. Rava: it's a tannaitic dispute, evidenced by differing counts of Temple treasurers

slides.title: 🧵 Can Priests Sleep on Vestments Containing Wool and Linen?
slides.subtitle: The diverse-kinds (kilayim) problem, worked through step by step

lines.speaker: Difficulty
lines.text: If priests placed their vestments literally UNDER their heads while sleeping, doesn't the belt (containing wool and linen) violate the kilayim prohibition — even if the Torah permits wearing it during service?

lines.speaker: Attempted defense
lines.text: Maybe kilayim only forbids WEARING the mixture, not lying upon it? But a baraita says even ten mattresses stacked atop a kilayim garment are forbidden to sleep on — the rabbinic decree applies regardless of actual risk.

lines.speaker: Resolution 1
lines.text: The mishna's 'beneath their heads' really means NEXT TO their heads, not literally underneath — avoiding the kilayim issue entirely.

lines.speaker: Resolution 2 (Rav Ashi)
lines.text: Priestly vestments, especially the belt, are STIFF — and the diverse-kinds prohibition applies only to soft, warmth-giving garments people derive comfort from, not stiff material like felt.

slides.title: 👑 Shimon HaTzaddik and Alexander the Great
slides.subtitle: Resolving whether priestly garments may be worn for ordinary benefit
slides.label: The proof text:
slides.text: A baraita states that priestly vestments may be worn anywhere WITHIN the Temple — even not during service — because 'priestly vestments were given for [ordinary] enjoyment,' but wearing them OUTSIDE the Temple, 'in the country,' is forbidden. Yet a well-known account has Shimon HaTzaddik greeting Alexander the Macedonian while dressed in the priestly vestments, outside the Temple, averting its destruction. Two resolutions: perhaps his garments merely RESEMBLED priestly vestments without being consecrated; or, if they truly were consecrated, the extraordinary circumstance justified overriding the normal halakha under the principle 'It is time to act for the Lord; they have nullified Your Torah' (Psalms 119:126).

slides.title: 🚽 Modesty, Health, and Etiquette — Practical Wisdom Passed to Sons
slides.subtitle: Framed by a memorable story about Rav Safra and Rabbi Abba

steps.content: 1️⃣ Story: Rav Safra was in the (doorless) bathroom; Rabbi Abba coughed to signal his presence. Rav Safra said 'enter' — but the mishna's privacy protocol suggests he shouldn't have! Rav Safra explains: he feared for Rabbi Abba's health if he had to wait

2️⃣ Rav to his son Ḥiyya, and Rav Huna to his son Rabba: relieve yourself at dawn and dusk (streets are empty then) so you're never forced to hold it in during the day, which risks health — and always sit before uncovering, cover before standing
3️⃣ When drinking wine: rinse the cup before AND after; with water, just pour some out before passing the cup to a student
4️⃣ A tragic precedent: a student too refined to drink from an unrinsed cup died of thirst rather than drink after his teacher — hence the enduring rule to always pour some out first
5️⃣ General etiquette: don't spit in your teacher's presence — except after gourds or porridge, whose saliva is dangerous (like molten metal) to hold in

summary.principle: The daf models how Temple protocol combines precise textual reconciliation (counting watch posts to the last person) with deep concern for human dignity and health — from where a watchman may sit, to whether a priest may rest his head on his own vestments, to a teacher's quiet instructions on basic bodily modesty.

flowSteps.content: 🔢 Levites' 21 posts reconciled against a 24-count verse via multiple approaches
🪑 Watch locations set by where sitting is permitted — Temple Mount inside, courtyard outside
🧵 Sleeping on vestments navigated around the kilayim prohibition through careful reinterpretation

columns.content: 👑 Priestly garments permitted for benefit inside the Temple, restricted outside — except in dire need
🚽 Bathroom and table etiquette taught as both practical health wisdom and interpersonal respect

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Temple law and everyday conduct share one concern — precise attention to dignity, whether of sacred property or of a person's body

quiz.q: How does the Gemara ultimately reconcile the biblical verse (I Chronicles 26:17–18), which seems to describe 24 watch posts, with the mishna's count of 21 Levite posts?
o: By declaring the verse an error

One approach: minor recount adjustments (the Parbar had only one actual watchman) bring it to 21; an alternative approach accepts 24 as accurate, with 3 of them being priestly posts described using the term 'Levites,' following Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle that priests are sometimes called Levites in Scripture
By assuming the mishna is mistaken and adopting 24 as the true number for Levites alone
There is no reconciliation offered
quiz.e: The Gemara offers two paths: adjusting the verse's count down to 21, or accepting 24 while attributing 3 posts to priests referred to by the term 'Levites' elsewhere in Scripture.

quiz.q: Why were the Levites' watch posts on the Temple Mount located INSIDE its wall, while their watch posts for the Temple courtyard were located OUTSIDE its wall?
o: It was purely random placement

Sitting is permitted on the Temple Mount, so watchmen could rest inside; sitting in the Temple courtyard is forbidden to all but Davidic kings, so watchmen were placed outside where they could sit if tired
The Temple Mount had no wall at all
Courtyard watchmen were considered more important and needed more space
quiz.e: The Gemara explains the placement is based entirely on where a tired watchman would be permitted to sit — inside the Mount's wall, but only outside the courtyard's wall, since courtyard sitting is reserved for Davidic royalty.

quiz.q: What is Rav Ashi's resolution to the problem of priests placing vestments containing wool and linen (kilayim) beneath their heads while sleeping?
o: He says this never actually happened
He explains that priestly vestments, especially the belt, are stiff, and the diverse-kinds prohibition applies only to soft garments that provide warmth and comfort, not stiff material
He says kilayim never applies to consecrated items
He says the vestments were made of a single material only
quiz.e: Rav Ashi's resolution is that the kilayim prohibition targets garments that give warmth and comfort, and stiff material like the priestly belt doesn't fall into that category.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's discussion of Shimon HaTzaddik meeting Alexander the Great while wearing priestly vestments outside the Temple, how is this reconciled with the rule forbidding wearing such vestments 'in the country'?
o: It cannot be reconciled; the story is rejected as false

Either his garments only resembled (but weren't actually) consecrated priestly vestments, or the extraordinary circumstance of averting the Temple's destruction justified overriding the halakha under 'it is time to act for the Lord'
The rule only applied after Shimon HaTzaddik's time
Alexander the Great was considered part of the Temple precincts
quiz.e: The Gemara offers two resolutions: the garments may not have been technically consecrated, or the extreme circumstances permitted overriding normal halakha for the sake of the Temple's survival.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rav and Rav Huna's advice to their sons, should a person relieve themselves at dawn and dusk even without urgent need?
o: Because it is considered more respectful to do so at those times
Because the streets are typically empty then, allowing privacy near one's home, so one won't be forced to hold it in during the busy daytime, which risks health
Because Jewish law requires it at those specific times
There is no such advice in the text
quiz.e: The advice reflects practical wisdom: relieving oneself at quiet times avoids the health risks of holding it in later when streets are crowded and privacy is harder to find.
